title: Having my own ideas
keyIdea: Young children learn by having their own ideas and trying them out, not only by copying. Copying a grown-up is a good start; then they change it to make it theirs: a tower in new colours, a den made a different way from the same chairs and blanket, a new rule for a game. When an idea does not work, they look at what went wrong and try a new way. Saying the idea out loud (I will try it this way) helps them plan and share it.

kid: You can copy a tower. That is a good start. Then you can make your own tower, your way. It can look different. Different is good!
Chairs and a blanket can make a den. A table and a sheet can make a den too. The same things can make lots of dens. You pick.
Games can have new rules. Kick the ball, do not roll it. Stand far back. Hop, do not run. You can make up a rule!
Ideas do not always work at first. My tower fell down. I tried big blocks at the bottom. Now it stands up! Say your idea: I will try it this way.
adult: England's EYFS framework names three ways children learn. One is creating and thinking critically. That means children have and develop their own ideas, make links between ideas, and find ways of doing things. Development Matters (2021) puts it under having their own ideas: thinking of ideas, finding ways to solve problems and finding new ways to do things. For 3 and 4 year olds it says they develop their own ideas and then decide which materials to use. In the US, the Head Start Early Learning Outcomes Framework lists creativity under Approaches to Learning.

Copying comes first, and that is fine. A child copies your tower and learns how blocks stack. Then they change one thing. That change is their idea. Open things like boxes, cloth and blocks give more room for ideas than a kit with one right answer. Trying an idea is a small test. The child does it, looks, and changes it. Talking helps too. When they say I will try it this way, they plan it.

Common mistakes to watch for: showing the one right way too soon (in one study, 4 year olds who were shown a single function of a toy explored it less than those who were not told); fixing the den for them when it falls; stopping play because it is messy; praising only copies of your own model; and treating a failed idea as a failure, when it is part of trying. Ask, Tell me about your idea, and wait.

In the lab your child copies a grown-up's tower, then builds their own that is different, makes three different dens from the same frames and covers, adds two new rules to a ball game, and picks a new way when a tower falls and a bridge is too short. Every step works by tapping big buttons or the pictures. Read the Challenge aloud together.

familyTip: Put out 3 cushions, a blanket and some pegs. Say, Let's make a den, and then wait. Do not show how. If it falls, ask, What could we try now? Next time, ask your child to make up one new rule for a game you both know.

visual.caption: A new idea or the same as before? Drag each one, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: Hop in tag, do not run
Build my tower just like yours
Kick the ball, do not roll it

lab.caption: Flagship lab: copy a tower, build your own, make three different dens, add new rules to a game and try a new way when an idea does not work.

practice.prompt: Sam builds his tower his own way. It is not like yours. Is that OK?
choices: No, it must be the same
practice.explain: Yes. His tower is his own idea. Different is good.

practice.prompt: You make {n} dens. Each one is a different way. How many den ideas did you have?
practice.hint: Each den is one idea. Count the dens.

practice.prompt: Your tower has {n} blocks. You add {a} more for your new idea. How many blocks now?
practice.hint: Start at {n} and count on {a} more.

practice.prompt: Your den falls down. What can you do?
practice.hint: Ideas do not always work the first time.
practice.explain: Look at what fell and try a new way. That is how ideas get better.

pool.prompt: Which is a new rule for tag?
pool.hint: A new rule changes something in the game.
pool.explain: Hopping changes the game, so it is a new rule. Running is the old way.

pool.prompt: Is it OK to copy first?
pool.hint: Copying is a start. What can you do next?
pool.explain: Copy first to learn how. Then change one thing to make it your idea.

pool.prompt: My tower keeps falling down. What could I try?
pool.hint: What makes a tower strong at the bottom?
pool.explain: Big blocks at the bottom make the tower strong. More on top makes it wobble.

pool.prompt: How can you tell people your idea?
choices: Say: I will try it this way
pool.hint: How do people know what you think?
pool.explain: Say it out loud. Then people can help, and you can make a plan.

pool.prompt: Lily makes a mess when she tries her box idea. What helps?
choices: Let her try, then tidy together
pool.hint: Is mess part of making things?
pool.explain: Mess is part of trying an idea. Let her finish, then tidy up together.

pool.prompt: You try {n} ways to fix the bridge. The last way works. How many ways did not work?
pool.hint: Take away the one way that worked.
pool.explain: {n} ways take away the 1 that worked leaves {=n-1}. Each try helped you find it.

pool.prompt: Which one is a new idea?
pool.hint: Which one did nobody show you?
pool.explain: A box hat for teddy is a new idea. The others are the same as before.

pool.prompt: You have {a} ideas for a game. You try {b} of them. How many ideas are left to try?
pool.hint: Start at {a} and take away the {b} you tried.
pool.explain: {a} ideas take away {b} tried leaves {=a-b} more to try.

pool.prompt: The bridge is too short. What could you try?
pool.hint: What can reach across the gap?
pool.explain: A longer block can reach across. Pushing the sides apart makes the gap bigger.
